episode.title: Frame the Decision: Pragmatic Threat Models

feed.description: Software engineering conversations: reliability, architecture, delivery, and the tradeoffs nobody puts in the blog post.
feed.title: Practical Systems

bullets: Embedded security ownership beats a central security gatekeeper — a position reversed after the 2024 webhook incident, having previously argued for a single central security team.
Threat modeling is a framing exercise rather than a checklist; frame the decision wrong and you build the wrong defenses, but once internalized the rest of the decisions get easier.
Authn/authz separation matters more than people think — a pattern observed holding across three different teams.
Security incidents are reliability incidents; ignoring that overlap means rebuilding the approach from scratch a year later, and the second-order effects are the part most people miss.
Vanta-style compliance work and real security work overlap only about 60% — passing compliance is not the same as being secure.
The frame for a security review is 'what could go wrong if this assumption is wrong' — the framing matters because it reveals which trade-offs you're making.
Tooling like PagerDuty, Datadog, and Sentry makes security trade-offs visible; outside of Sentry-class tooling, the failure mode is harder to spot.
Risk management cross-cuts every security design trade-off; the practical starting point is picking one idea and running it for two weeks, then iterating.
